title: De insigni paradoxo, quod in analysi maximorum et minimorum occurrit

deep.reconstruction:
Problem served (set up on p.17): find the curve EY, referred to a vertical axis AC, such that the integral ∫ √x ds is a minimum. Here x is the vertical distance YV of the curve point below the horizontal line AB, and ds = dx√(1+p²) with p = dy/dx. Euler reads this as Maupertuis' action ∫ v ds with v ∝ √x, so he expects the projectile path, a parabola.

On this page Euler uses his Methodus (1744) rule. For ∫ V dx with dV = M dx + N dy + P dp, the extremal satisfies N dx = dP. Here V = √(x(1+p²)), which gives M = √(1+p²)/(2√x), N = 0 and P = p√x/√(1+p²). Since N = 0, P is constant, written √a; this is the first integral for a cyclic coordinate y.

§5: Solving gives p²(x−a) = a, so p = √(a/(x−a)) and dy = √a dx/√(x−a). Integrating, y = 2√(a(x−a)) + b, i.e. (y−b)² = 4a(x−a). This is a parabola with vertical axis, vertex E at depth AE = a below AB, focal distance a and parameter 4a. Euler states the result as: vertex distance from AB equals the focal distance. In modern words, AB is the common directrix of all extremals. This is the familiar fact that every trajectory launched with given energy has its directrix at the zero-velocity level.

§6: Along the extremal √(1+p²) = √(x/(x−a)), so ds = √x dx/√(x−a). The integrand to be minimised becomes x dx/√(x−a). The next page integrates this to (2/3)(x+2a)√(x−a) and then exhibits the paradox: the broken path E→A→V→Y runs along AB, where √x = 0 and the integrand costs nothing. Its value (2/3)(a^{3/2}+x^{3/2}) beats the parabola for large x.
errors: No substantive error on this page. P=const, p=√(a/(x−a)), y=2√(ax−aa)+b and ds=√x dx/√(x−a) are all correct; the next page's integral (2/3)(x+2a)√(x−a) also checks.
Minor omissions: the sign choice ±p (the other branch of the parabola) is ignored. The degenerate constant a=0 (vertical straight lines, p infinite) is not discussed.
The print has 'p = y/∂x' (missing ∂ in the numerator); the transcription silently corrects this to ∂y/∂x.

ideas.what: First integral of the Euler–Lagrange equation when the integrand does not contain y (N=0 ⇒ P = ∂F/∂p constant)
ideas.modern_name: Conservation law for a cyclic variable / first integral of the Euler–Lagrange equation
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (1744), ch. 2–3

ideas.what: Extremals of ∫√x ds are parabolas whose common directrix is the line x=0 (vertex distance = focal distance)
ideas.modern_name: Projectile trajectories at fixed energy have their directrix at the zero-kinetic-energy level; Jacobi–Maupertuis metric √(E−U) ds
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (projectile/directrix property known since the 17th c.; Euler's use of the least-action form 1744)
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum II (motion of projectiles by least action, 1744)

ideas.what: Computation of the action density along the extremal, preparing the comparison with a broken path through the zero-cost boundary
ideas.modern_name: Failure of minimality of extremals (conjugate points/envelope) and Goldschmidt-type discontinuous solutions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jacobi (1837) for conjugate points; Goldschmidt (1831) for discontinuous solutions of the minimal surface of revolution; Weierstrass for the field theory
ideas.where_published: This paper E735 (Mém. Acad. St-Pétersbourg III, 1811); I believe its paradox is discussed in histories of the calculus of variations (Todhunter 1861 / Goldstine 1980 — unsure of exact treatment)

deep.surprise_reason: This page is a routine Euler–Lagrange derivation leading to the directrix parabola family. The interesting content, an early Goldschmidt-like broken comparison path showing an extremal that is not minimal, is on the following page. That paradox is the published point of E735 and is, as far as I know, noted in histories of the calculus of variations, so nothing here appears missing from the record.
transcription_corrections: In the image §5 reads 'p = y/∂x' (a printing slip for ∂y/∂x); the transcription gives the intended p = ∂y/∂x.
The line break 'ae-/haec' visible in the scan belongs to 'unde / haec deducitur aequatio'; the transcription is correct as given.
